interactions: Vancomycin + cefepime: no pharmacokinetic interaction; monitor renal function, since vancomycin is nephrotoxic and cefepime accumulates when renal function falls.
Vancomycin + dexamethasone: corticosteroids may reduce vancomycin penetration into CSF as meningeal inflammation subsides; dose vancomycin to serum levels.

Vancomycin + trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole: trimethoprim raises serum creatinine by blocking its tubular secretion and can cause hyperkalaemia; additive renal monitoring is needed when interpreting vancomycin dosing.

Cefepime or meropenem + levetiracetam: no pharmacokinetic interaction; both beta-lactams can lower the seizure threshold (cefepime neurotoxicity mainly with renal impairment), so continue seizure prophylaxis.

prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT attribute turbid CSF with Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain and a CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.19 to post-surgical chemical meningitis: positive microbiological results establish bacterial infection and require antibiotic treatment.
Do NOT delay empirical IV antibiotics while awaiting culture results or imaging.

Do NOT use community-acquired empirical cover (ceftriaxone, with or without vancomycin) without an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam: Gram-negative bacilli cause a significant proportion of post-neurosurgical CNS infections (IDSA 2017).
Do NOT omit source control: leaving the infected EVD in place risks treatment failure.
required_recommendations: Draw two sets of peripheral blood cultures before the first therapeutic antibiotic dose.

Sample CSF from the EVD sampling port, not the drain bag, before the first therapeutic antibiotic dose and send cell count with differential, glucose with paired blood glucose, protein, lactate, Gram stain, culture with susceptibility and multiplex PCR.

Give vancomycin 15 to 20 mg/kg IV every 8 to 12 hours, dosed to serum levels, plus cefepime 2 g IV every 8 hours or meropenem 2 g IV every 8 hours within 60 minutes, after cultures and without waiting for imaging (IDSA 2017).
Remove or replace the EVD as soon as antibiotics have started (IDSA 2017).

Obtain a non-contrast CT head for the fall in consciousness with an EVD in situ, and a contrast-enhanced MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for ventriculitis, abscess and empyema; neither may delay antibiotics.
Monitor vancomycin levels, creatinine and potassium every 48 to 72 hours while she also takes trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and dexamethasone.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: for methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, change to nafcillin or oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours and stop vancomycin and the anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (IDSA 2017).

avoided_actions.rationale: ECG does not contribute to the diagnosis or management of healthcare-associated ventriculitis and meningitis.

No clinical features of endocarditis and no bacteraemia (blood cultures no growth); echocardiography is not part of the ventriculitis work-up unless Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia or a valvular source is found.
No arrhythmia indication; continuous cardiac monitoring contributes nothing to the diagnosis or treatment of ventriculitis.
Amyloid PET is a dementia biomarker with no role in acute infectious meningitis.
FDG-PET is not indicated in acute healthcare-associated ventriculitis; CT and MRI cover the relevant indications.

accepted: Healthcare-associated (post-neurosurgical) bacterial meningitis and ventriculitis due to Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), EVD-associated

differential.key_features: Blood products after craniotomy cause pleocytosis, raised protein and RBCs in CSF; excluded as the sole cause by Gram-positive cocci in clusters on Gram stain, Staphylococcus aureus in culture, a glucose ratio of 0.19 and CSF lactate 7.2 mmol/L.

differential.diagnosis: Nosocomial Gram-negative bacillary meningitis or ventriculitis (e.g., Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Klebsiella pneumoniae)
differential.key_features: Gram-negative bacilli cause a significant share of post-neurosurgical infections and are covered empirically; excluded here by Gram-positive cocci in clusters on Gram stain and Staphylococcus aureus alone in culture.

Coagulase-negative staphylococci are the commonest EVD pathogens and also appear as Gram-positive cocci in clusters, usually with a more indolent course; culture identifies Staphylococcus aureus instead.
Known glioblastoma and leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI raise it, but the acute neutrophilic CSF with Staphylococcus aureus in culture explains the findings.
No erythema, purulence or dehiscence at the craniotomy or EVD exit site; the ventricular CSF shows intracranial infection.

differential.diagnosis: Community-acquired bacterial meningitis (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis)
differential.key_features: In-situ EVD after neurosurgery; S. pneumoniae and N. meningitidis not detected by multiplex PCR, and culture grows Staphylococcus aureus.

key_clinical_evidence: Pleocytosis is expected after craniotomy and can mimic bacterial meningitis; after neurosurgery CSF cell count, glucose and protein are less reliable and CSF culture is the key test, with Gram stain, CSF lactate and procalcitonin as support (IDSA 2017). Here the Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters, the glucose ratio is 0.19 and the CSF lactate 7.2 mmol/L.

EVD-associated infection has a nosocomial spectrum dominated by staphylococci (MRSA, MSSA, coagulase-negative) and Gram-negative bacilli, so empirical cover is vancomycin plus an anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, ceftazidime or meropenem), not a community-acquired regimen (IDSA 2017).

The CSF RBC count (310 cells/microL) reflects postoperative blood products, not a new hemorrhage; this chemical-meningitis red herring does not account for the Gram-positive cocci on stain or the markedly low CSF glucose.
Infected ventricular drains are removed or replaced as part of treatment (IDSA 2017); antibiotics alone risk failure.

The commercial multiplex meningitis PCR panel does not target Staphylococcus aureus or Gram-negative bacilli other than E. coli K1, so a negative panel does not exclude healthcare-associated ventriculitis; culture identifies the organism.

Her maintenance dexamethasone may reduce vancomycin CSF penetration; vancomycin is dosed to serum levels, and intraventricular therapy is considered if the response to systemic therapy is poor (IDSA 2017).
A raised serum procalcitonin (3.6 ng/mL here) supports bacterial infection rather than purely local chemical irritation, though it is not specific after surgery.
MRI ependymal enhancement adjacent to the EVD catheter tip localises the infection to the ventricles (ventriculitis).

Blood cultures show no growth, so there is no Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia and no indication for echocardiography; the infection was acquired on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis, so the specimens were not antimicrobial-naive.

red_herrings.intended_effect: Frame the current fever on day 8 as a continuation of expected post-surgical fever, anchoring away from new infectious etiology and delaying microbiological evaluation.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Blood products after craniotomy raise the CSF RBC count and can cause a sterile chemical pleocytosis, but Gram-positive cocci in clusters on Gram stain, a CSF:blood glucose ratio of 0.19, a CSF lactate of 7.2 mmol/L and Staphylococcus aureus in culture establish bacterial ventriculitis regardless of the RBCs.

Sampling an EVD carries no herniation risk, so it does not wait for the CT, and the CT must not delay sampling or antibiotics.

patient.history_present_illness: This is a 44-year-old right-handed woman with recently diagnosed right parietal glioblastoma who underwent gross total resection via right parietal craniotomy eight days ago. An external ventricular drain (EVD) was placed intraoperatively for perioperative intracranial pressure monitoring and has remained in situ. Her postoperative course was initially unremarkable: she was extubated on the day of surgery, her GCS returned to 15 by postoperative day 2, and she had mild stable left hemiparesis consistent with the surgical bed. Concurrent temozolomide chemoradiation was planned to start once the wound had healed, and her dexamethasone was being tapered. On postoperative day 6 she developed a temperature of 37.9°C that was attributed by the neurosurgery team to expected post-craniotomy fever and wound healing. Repeat CT head on day 6 showed expected postoperative changes with blood products at the resection cavity and no new mass effect. No antibiotics were started at that time. On the morning of postoperative day 8, nursing staff noted that she had become progressively lethargic over the preceding 12 hours, was difficult to rouse for morning medications, and her GCS had declined to 13. The CSF collected from the EVD drain bag had changed in appearance from clear to turbid and faintly yellow-green. She complained of headache and neck stiffness when asked. Her temperature was recorded as 38.6°C. On examination, she demonstrated nuchal rigidity with positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs; these signs were absent in the immediate postoperative period.

neurological_exam.additional: Nuchal rigidity present on passive neck flexion — patient grimaces and resists neck flexion. Kernig sign positive on the right. Positive Brudzinski sign. EVD catheter in situ via right parietal entry site; drain site dressing intact, no visible purulence or erythema at skin entry. CSF from EVD reservoir is turbid and faintly yellow-green, distinct from the clear CSF observed in the immediate postoperative period. Temperature 38.6°C. No skin rash or petechiae.
neurological_exam.coordination: Cannot fully assess due to lethargy; finger-nose intact on right.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, equally reactive to light. No papilledema on bedside fundoscopy. Extraocular movements intact. No facial asymmetry. Corneal reflexes present. No evidence of new cranial nerve palsy.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Lethargic and slow to respond. Oriented to person and place but unable to state the correct date. Follows simple one-step commands only. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). Baseline postoperative GCS on hospital day 2 was 15 with full orientation; today represents a clear decline.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild left hemiparesis (4/5 upper and lower extremity) consistent with known right parietal resection; no change from postoperative day 2 motor exam. No new focal deficits identified. Tone mildly increased in the left upper extremity.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps and brachioradialis 2+ on the right, 3+ on the left. Patellar 2+ on the right, 3+ on the left. Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Left plantar response extensor (Babinski); right plantar flexor — consistent with prior resection.
neurological_exam.sensory: Decreased light touch and pinprick in the left upper extremity consistent with right parietal territory — no change from baseline postoperative exam.
